mappings.note: Sodium and potassium named as the knife-soft metals: materials identified by a property.
Names rust, the brown deposit itself. The item about the process that makes it is mapped to LO-37.
Names rusting as the process, not the deposit, and in this chapter the process is defined by the air-and-water conditions that cause it.
Water and air together as the requirements for rusting: the phenomenon tied to its causes.
Corrosion as decay through reaction with air, water or other substances; the definition is itself causal.
The dazzling white flame is what the student sees in the demonstration, so the observation outcome rather than LO-39, where the product is named.
Metal oxides as generally basic: a property assigned to a whole class of materials.
Non-metal oxides as generally acidic, the class-level counterpart.
Names phosphorus from the fact that it is kept under water because it ignites in air. Plain identification here, unlike the multiple-choice version where four candidates had to be told apart.
Element as a substance that cannot be broken down further, the category that metals and non-metals divide.
Oxygen as the non-metal needed for breathing: importance in life, so the application outcome.
Explains malleability, with foil offered as illustration. The definition carries the marks, so LO-33 rather than LO-45.
Coal and sulfur are called brittle precisely because they shatter where metals flatten, so the answer rests on the contrast with metals.
Explains ductility, with wiring as the illustration. Like the malleability item, the property definition is what is assessed.
Sonority identifies a metal only against the dull sound of wood or coal, so this is the metal-versus-non-metal discrimination rather than the bare property name.
Metal cooking vessels because metals conduct heat: property behind an everyday object.
Wooden or plastic handles as insulation against burns, the companion everyday application.
Rubber gloves protect an electrician from shock: insulation applied to a real occupation.
Tells metals from non-metals by whether the tester bulb glows, an explicit differentiation on a property.
Defines corrosion and asks for an example beyond rust, such as the green film on copper. The definition is causal, so LO-37 rather than LO-33.
Asks what happens and what product forms when magnesium burns, which is the metal plus oxygen reaction. Not LO-36, since the product rather than the observation carries the answer.
How to show magnesium oxide is basic: dissolve it and test with litmus. The item asks for the procedure and its evidence, so LO-36.
Burning sulfur gives sulfur dioxide, which with water gives sulfurous acid: two reactions and their products.
How to show the sulfur solution is acidic, i.e. the litmus test and its reading, matching the magnesium oxide procedure item.
Sodium is kept under kerosene because it reacts violently with air and water: the practice is traced to the cause. Not LO-45, because no everyday problem is being solved.
Two properties that separate metals from non-metals, the differentiation outcome in its plainest form.
Two non-metals with a use for each: the item is built on uses, so the application outcome.
Defines metallic lustre as the shine of a fresh or polished metal surface, an observable feature.
Steel rope in bridges and cranes justified by strength and ductility: property behind a real use.
Rules plastic, glass and wood out of the element category because they are combinations of elements, which is classification by composition.
Compares metals and non-metals across four properties at once, the fullest differentiation item in the chapter.
Describes both burning experiments (LO-36) and then contrasts the basic and acidic oxides they yield (LO-34). Both halves are demanded by the question.
Names malleability as the property used and explains why heating is needed to exploit it: the smith's practice traced to its cause. Not LO-45, since no material choice is being made.
Justifies copper or aluminium for the conductor and plastic or rubber for the sheath, a property-driven design decision in daily life.
The Iron Pillar and what its condition says about ancient Indian metallurgy is a story of scientific achievement. Not LO-45, since no prevention method is required in the answer.
Three properties behind the choice of gold and silver for jewellery: properties applied to a use.
Defines element, divides elements into metals and non-metals and rules other materials out: classification throughout.
Argues the importance of oxygen, carbon, nitrogen and chlorine for life and technology: a use-centred answer.
Why rusting matters and two ways to stop it, which is the preventing-corrosion application. The damage half is framing for the prevention the answer must give.
The student runs a hammer test and a conduction test (LO-36) and then decides which cubes are metals (LO-35). Both the evidence and the sorting are asked for.
Aluminium against galvanised iron for a humid coastal site is a corrosion-resistance decision about real construction, so LO-45 rather than LO-34.
Decides whether a sample is really gold from lustre, malleability, ductility and acid resistance: a material identified from its observable properties.

Kerosene works as a storage medium only because it keeps water and air off the sodium, so the item turns on why the precaution works. Not LO-45, since laboratory storage is not a day-to-day application.
States the general rule that metal oxides are basic and non-metal oxides acidic: a class-level generalisation drawn from the two litmus results.
